title: Add support for multi-threading/multi-processing in Streamlit
body:
### 👀 EDIT: See [response from Streamlit team below](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8490#issuecomment-2060387813) and request for feedback! 🎈 

### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Whenever I have tried adding multi-threading to the Streamlit app, it gives me an error and if I can resolve the error then it complains about st.sesssin_session having no key.

Error messages:
“Thread ‘Thread-1_0’: missing ScriptContext”
To resolve the above error, I have added the following lines:
`from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import add_script_run_ctx
t1 = threading.Thread(target=target, args=args)
add_script_run_ctx(t1)
`
If I add the above code then it does not give the error but then I get the following error even if the target function has the logic of adding the result to the session key
"st.session_state has no key "<key_name>". Did you forget to initialize it?"



### Why?

It always comes to the performance when the user is interacting with the data-intensive application. The main idea behind this feature is to add support for the multi-processing using native `Threading` or `concurrent.futures`. This will help the developers to use this and load the data or time-consuming code snippets run in parallel. This is one of the best features that streamlit can add to improve the performance and efficiency of the app. 

### How?

While I am not 100% sure, something like `st.experimental_thread` or `st.experimental_concurrent` decorator on top of Python's `concurrent.futures` functionality with similar parameters.

### Additional Context


**Related issues:**
- https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/1326

I do have a package in alpha that lets you run sub-processes pretty easily. It's not the same thing as threading but can definitely help in some circumstances. https://libraries.io/pypi/streamlit-process-manager

Thanks [USER] and folks who responded. I know there are many other Github issues in the past with related requests too :) Here's the semi-official response and status on this:

1. We recognize it's a long term challenge with building complex apps with Streamlit, and one that has been seeming to come up even more frequently too as Streamlit is used for a widening set of use cases and contexts.
2. To that end, if folks have other packages or best practices on what is possible today, we'd love to amplify - [streamlit-process-manager](https://libraries.io/pypi/streamlit-process-manager) is a great example, I had fun hacking together some examples with it! I also wonder if `st.experimental_fragment` can help here short term.
3. A number of folks on the Streamlit team are thinking about this and interested in providing better support. However it's not a short term top priority - not something we're likely to tackle in the next 3-4 months. But hopefully in the next big push after that (at least personally I'm advocating for that! We'll see)

**Here are some thoughts / request for feedback on how it might work, would love input and responses from anyone!**

### Use cases?

Thinking about 3 main scenarios for this currently:
- **Long running compute in the same process:** This seems to be the same use case described in the original issue. Say I have a RAG pipeline and some documents being indexed to an in-memory vector store. I'd like to run it in a separate thread so the user can continue interacting.
- **Waiting for a slow database call:** I ran something in a connected database (or similar), such as kicking off a Task / sproc in Snowflake or storing some embeddings in an outside vector store. Would be nice if the app isn't stuck while waiting for that to complete.
- **Waiting for a webhook callback from an external service:** Maybe I submitted an async request to a third party API like Twilio, Stripe, etc and I'd like to notify the user when it completes. Whenever we add #439, it would support a callback webhook. But then I need to also async call back into the running user session to update the app when that happens.

Are there others folks have in mind?

### Requirements

Seems like key ones are:
- I can get some information from the async thread back into the session_state of a relevant session
- I can trigger an `st.rerun()` (or fragment rerun) based on something happening in an async thread, not just user interaction.
- (?) I can interrupt an async thread based on some user action (like pressing a "cancel" button or even closing the session prematurely)

Are there any others?

### API or pseudo-code sketches ???

Would love to hear ideas here. One idea would just be "make the normal async / asyncio stuff just work!". But I think there might be some streamlit-specific parts that would be useful too. Also if you know other libraries that you especially like how they integrate this, would love to hear about it. I also have a couple of ideas but want to hear y'all's first!

Another use case is using LangChain/LangGraph.  Invoking a runnable often creates new threads (under the hood), which causes a ScriptRunContext error when using StreamlitCallbackHandler.  As LangChain is, what I image to be, a core use-case of Streamlit - we need to think of a solution.

[see related issue](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/issues/101)

I have a barcode scanner hooked to a network, and I am having lots of trouble getting the scanner to update the streamlit fields with data. Something like this feature request would be ideal.

One other workaround is to use Python to open a browser to perform the text field manipulations, and the other is to use fragments in combination with a shared file/DB to periodically check for updates.

What's really frustrating is I see the command line output for streamlit recognize when the file has changed (using TinyDB) but then ignore it. If only I could hook into that watchdog thread and run a fragment on the ignored changes. Then at least we could use a file update as the refresh trigger, which is a cleaner workaround than a browser hack or refresh loop.

Hi, I've found a way to combine threading & fragment to get a fairly responsive behavior. 

Note: the example below is just one way of using this technique; I have since moved to another more complicated variation, but this is the most straight forward one: (Thanks mainly to the SO answer, and what jcarroll showed me in another exchange.)

Hope the Streamlit team can package the 'run_in_thread' decorator up somehow.

```
import time
from functools import wraps
from threading import Thread

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

import streamlit as st
from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import add_script_run_ctx, get_script_run_ctx


## function wrapper
def run_in_thread(func):
    # per https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76472211/multithreading-for-streamlit-and-kite-connect
    [USER](func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        thread = Thread(target=func, args=args, kwargs=kwargs)
        ctx = get_script_run_ctx()
        add_script_run_ctx(thread, ctx)
        thread.start()
    return wrapper


# this is a fn that takes time to complete, (e.g. database call, etc.)
# so we run it in a thread
[USER]_in_thread
def generate_data(x=1, sleep=2):  # example from j.carroll
    print('in generate data fn')
    time.sleep(sleep)  # simulating the delay
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        np.random.randn(5, 5) * x, columns=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
    )
    print(f'returning df after sleep.. len={len(df)}')
    st.session_state.df = df


LOAD_FREQ = 10
[USER].fragment(run_every=1)
def update_data():
    print('in update data fn')
    load_timer = st.session_state.load_timer
    now = time.monotonic()
    if now > load_timer + LOAD_FREQ:
        # avoid generating data all the time
        print('update data now > timer + freq')
        st.session_state.load_timer = now
        generate_data()


[USER].fragment(run_every=1)
def filter_data(min_idx):
    print('in filter data fn')
    df = st.session_state.df
    st.session_state.df_f = df[df.index >= min_idx].copy()


[USER].fragment(run_every=1)
def draw_graph(graph_slot):
    print('in draw graph fn')
    df = st.session_state.df_f
    if df is not None:
        graph_slot.plotly_chart(px.bar(df))


def init_states():
    if 'df' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.df = pd.DataFrame()
        st.session_state.df_f = pd.DataFrame()
    if 'load_timer' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.load_timer = time.monotonic()


def main():
    init_states()
    "`generate_data()` runs in the background, so these widgets remain fully interactive"
    st.button("Button 1")
    st.slider("Random slider", 0, 100)

    min_idx = st.selectbox('min idx', range(0, 5))
    graph_slot = st.empty()

    update_data()
    filter_data(min_idx)
    draw_graph(graph_slot)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

```

Thanks everyone for the rich discussion here. 🙏 Over time this issue has become a catch-all for several *distinct* needs, and most of them now have clearer, dedicated homes. To keep the conversation focused and actionable, we're closing this in favor of the more specific issues below — please 👍 and continue in whichever one matches your use case:

- **Loading independent sections / data in parallel to speed up a page** → use `st.fragment(parallel=True)`. Independent sections run concurrently and render into reserved containers, so total load time is the slowest section rather than the sum. See [Run fragments in parallel](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/fragments#run-fragments-in-parallel) (and the [`st.fragment` API reference](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/execution-flow/st.fragment)).

- **Long-running or non-blocking background work** — e.g. kicking off a slow computation or database/API call, updating the app when it finishes, or cancelling in-flight work → **#6687** (background execution).

- **Reacting to external events / webhooks** — receiving external HTTP calls is now supported via custom routes on **`st.App`** (the ASGI/Starlette integration, #439, available since 1.53 and the default in 1.57; feedback in #13600). Pushing such an event into a running session to update the UI is tracked in **#6687**.

- **CPU-bound work / `multiprocessing` / `ProcessPoolExecutor`** → tracked separately in **#4788** and **#7851**.

A note on calling `st.*` from your own or a library's threads: this remains unsupported and is not thread-safe — elements can arrive in the UI in an unpredictable order. For concurrency that renders as part of your app, use parallel fragments (which render into reserved containers). For work whose result you want to surface when it finishes, follow **#6687** — getting a completed background task to update the UI (rather than polling for it) is part of what that issue covers.

If your specific need isn't captured by any of the above, please open a new issue so we can track it! Thanks again for all the input here! 🎈
